channel.title: On Foot — Walking Tour Notes
channel.description: Guided walking tours in London and further afield, written up from notes and photographed for Getty Images.

item.title: Reading the Wood Without Leaves — SE London · Sydenham Hill Wood, SE26
item.description: Blackthorn that blossoms before it leafs, black ash buds, a boundary tree that proves girth is no guide to age, and why dead oaks are left standing and brash is stacked into dead hedges. Ends on the old Crystal Palace railway as the light goes. My notes begin partway through the walk.

item.title: Below Stairs at Gunnersbury — W London · Gunnersbury Park, W3
item.description: A smoke jack that turned the roast, a cold cupboard filled with park ice, a butchery that may or may not have been built for kosher cooking, and two French chefs the family paid well enough to keep. Plus a Rothschild wedding upstairs, a family motto, and the pigeons that were real — even if the Waterloo story is not.

item.title: Rough Seas, Indoors — South Kensington · Imperial College London, SW7
item.description: A lab built to make the sea — walked from a teaching bench where students try to catch wave theory out, past a glass flume, a snake-moving wall of paddles and a GPS-denied catamaran, to a turtle robot, a plesiosaur that learned to swim for David Attenborough in four months, and a hundred-year North Sea storm on demand.

item.title: The Fortress Nobody Bothered to Modernise — Sirmione · Lake Garda, Lombardy, Italy
item.description: A four-kilometre peninsula walked from its Scaliger castle — intact because it was demoted before gunpowder mattered — past 166 Cathars burned in Verona, a church whose walls were rented to the villagers, Callas's lakeside house and a Roman villa named for the wrong poet, to the glacier that left the rock standing.

item.title: The Wolf Islets and the Fortress That Changed Flags — Suomenlinna · Helsinki, Finland
item.description: A sea fortress built by Sweden, held by Russia and renamed by Finland — walked stop by stop from a church that doubles as a lighthouse and windows painted to save on glass, through a casemate where one in five soldiers died, to the courtyard where half the commandant's house was lost to a Crimean War bombardment.

item.title: A Capital Built to Look Like Somewhere Else — Helsinki · Senate Square to Citizens' Square, Finland
item.description: A town no Swedish noble wanted to live in becomes a tsar's showpiece capital — then the guide walks it from Engel's Senate Square past Agricola's alphabet, a scarred plinth, bricks borrowed from a demolished Åland fortress, a hug-sized Moomin, trolls guarding a doorway and the glass-and-granite new heart of the city, with a sauna and a bridge opened this April on the way.

item.title: A Wartime Hospital, a Dovecote & Britain's Secret Codebreakers — Eastcote · Field End Road, HA5
item.description: A ten-year local resident walks a farming hamlet turned suburb — from a farmhouse that became a 400-patient First World War hospital, past a Georgian house rebuilt by an Arts and Crafts pioneer, to the housing estate hiding one of Bletchley Park's most important codebreaking outstations.

item.title: The Arch, the Aylesham & What It Takes to Save a Street — Peckham · Rye Lane & Peckham High Street, SE15
item.description: Three local heritage groups walk a town centre still fighting for its own future — from a threatened 1990s canopy and Will Alsop's library on stilts, through a 1970s campaign that stopped a motorway, to the planning inspector's ruling against an 850-home tower scheme still headed for judicial review.

item.title: Soapsuds, a Stolen Park & the Return of Council Housing — South Acton & Mill Hill Park, W3
item.description: The guide walks South Acton on Ruskin's terms — from a bus garage that once fed a thousand workers, through "Soapsud Island" and a recreation ground residents fought to keep, to the Tenant Management Organisation now buying council homes back, and the Mill Hill Park garden suburb built deliberately to keep its distance.

item.title: Seven Kings, One Stone & the Tide That Turns — Kingston upon Thames · KT1
item.description: A walk through the Royal Borough's Saxon coronations, the sarsen stone recovered from a collapsed chapel, a bridge Thomas Wyatt's rebels had to rebuild before they could cross it, Bentalls' unlikely Hampton Court façade, and the dog buried on Clarence Street who became the face of His Master's Voice.

item.title: A Plague Pit, a Duke's Arrest & the Invention of Offside — Central London · Charterhouse Square, EC1M
item.description: The guide walks seven acres that have been a plague pit, a Carthusian priory, a Tudor mansion and an almshouse in turn — via a prior's arm nailed to the gate, a duke undone by a cipher hidden under a doormat, and the cloister where Charterhouse schoolboys may have invented football's offside rule.

item.title: From Cathedral Bells to a Sinking City — Jakarta · Indonesia
item.description: A neo-Gothic cathedral built twice, a mosque designed by a Christian architect, the old Stadhuis where two hundred people were killed in a single night in 1740, the last Dutch drawbridge in Batavia, and a national monument whose flame took fourteen years to light — ending, fittingly, on a stop about the fastest-sinking city on Earth.

item.title: The Largest Lizard on Earth and the Myth in Its Bite — Komodo National Park · Indonesia
item.description: A ten-hour boat loop through the national park: the 815-step climb up Padar for its three-coloured beaches, the foraminifera behind Pink Beach's sand, a ranger-led search for the dragons themselves — and the venom myth their bite finally put to rest in 2009, three years after the "just bacteria" story was disproven.

item.title: From Seabed to Sunlit Stone — Gua Batu Cermin · Labuan Bajo, Flores, Indonesia
item.description: A 75-metre limestone hill with coral in its walls, a Dutch priest who documented it in 1951 and opened up the Liang Bua "hobbit" cave, the noon light that gives the rock its name — and a quiet correction to the popular line that the cave itself was once underwater.

item.title: Cattle, Crowds & the Cally Tower — N London · Caledonian Park, N7
item.description: The two guides walk a market that once traded 15,000 animals a day, a field that hosted the largest political demonstrations in Georgian and Victorian London, the birthplace of Lord's cricket ground, and the 1852 world-record mile — before tracing the site's slow fall from cattle pens to a notorious council estate and back to a park with a tower you can climb.

item.title: 178 Steps to the Top — N London · Caledonian Park, N7
item.description: A different kind of tour of the same tower — climbed rather than walked around, led by the volunteers who wind its Victorian mechanism weekly. From the market's old banking office and public toilets, through a winding room housing a clock older than Big Ben, to a 360-degree view and one guide's own childhood memories of the derelict estate that used to stand beside it.

item.title: Nets, Tar & the Ghost of Dunkirk — Hastings Old Town · East Sussex
item.description: The guide walks the beach where Europe's largest beach-launched fishing fleet still works — from a church-turned-museum housing the last sailing boat built in Hastings, past tar-black net shops and a Dunkirk "ghost" lifeboat, to a lifeboat station funded by two bequeathed Ferraris and a Christmas charity founded on a winkle shell.

item.title: Shipwreck Houses, Smugglers' Cellars & a Butcher's Legend — Hastings Old Town · East Sussex
item.description: A looser, more anecdotal companion to the Stade walk — cottages built from shipwreck timber, a window-tax house with windows painted on, a smugglers' lantern-signal cottage, mummified cats in the oldest pub in town, and the persistent local legend that Sweeney Todd learned his trade in a Hastings butcher's shop.

item.title: Homes for People Who Kept Trying to Leave — E London · Bethnal Green to Hoxton
item.description: A chartered town planner walks the museum's own back streets — from a Georgian house where a Sephardic boxing champion once lived, through Victorian tenements built on early reinforced concrete, to the point block saved from demolition by Britain's first postwar heritage listing, and a mother-and-child sculpture raised as a small act of faith in a neighbourhood that kept losing people.

item.title: Nine Hundred Years, a Pie Full of Live Pigeons — Central London · Smithfield, EC1
item.description: A volunteer guide walks the North Wing James Gibbs built for free — Hogarth's staircase murals painted against a rival Venetian, a Charter Window etched with glaziers' names since 1652, a ceiling of poppies and gilded oak leaves, and the 12th-century vision that gave Rahere his hospital at Smithfield.
